utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would the registrar please call the matter for hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-66-PT, the Prosecutor versus Fatmir Limaj, Haradin Bala, and Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, my name is Andrew Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor with my colleagues to my right Mr. Alex Whiting, to his right Mr. Colin Black, and to my left is our case manager Mr. Hasan Younis. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I represent Fatmir Limaj together with my co-counsel, Karim Khan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I represent Haradin Bala. My co-counsel, Mr. Harvey, is at this time otherwise occupied in a matter in Great Britain. I am assisted by two legal assistants at this time, Ms. Nicola Walsh, and Ms. Caroline Buisman, and the gentleman sitting to go my right is Mr. Gentian Zyberi who is here for purposes of assisting all of the present accused for purposes of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. I represent Isak Musliu together with co-counsel Steven Powles and our legal assistant Michelle Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'm sorry things are a little squeezy this morning. I gather there were difficulties fitting everybody in, and I'm sorry for the delay in that matter being sorted. Now, this is the final pre-trial time that we assemble. I anticipate one matter. I have been just given to understand that there was this morning a recurrence of a matter raised by counsel with the Chamber when we were last together. That is concerning the circumstances in which the accused are brought into the Tribunal. I had been assured as late as this morning that the ministry had given instructions that there would be no repetition of that matter. There is no need for any further submission at the moment in respect of it. The matter will be taken up by the Chamber itself in the course of the day to see how the result was not in accordance with the word that was passed to the Registry by the ministry. Now, I've gone that far just to enable the translation to proceed, and I inquire now of the three accused whether they are able to understand the proceedings in the language that it is being interpreted in to them. Can I ask first of Mr. Limaj whether that is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED LIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bala.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BALA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Musliu.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MUSLIU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. It's clear to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Cayley, is there matter which the Prosecution wishes to raise at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I expect you will be addressing me at some stage on the matters that we need to specifically address under the Rules to the Pre-Trial Conference, but I leave that in your hands for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was inviting you to take up those matters that affect you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Nothing affects me at the moment, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you're not expecting me to call on you specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm not Your Honour, no, unless there is something specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As long as we understand each other, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may indicate the topics at the moment. The first is a further opportunity to address the Tribunal concerning the question of postponement, which was raised at a conference last week, because documentation arrived late on Thursday, and Friday, as you know, was a holiday, and it hasn't been possible to enter a further response. We did put a response in but in fact they crossed, as it were. But I would be grateful for a further opportunity to address you about that. As the question of blindfolds apparently is resolved, nothing more on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But don't tempt fate, Mr. Mansfield, but it's under consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The further matter is, and perhaps I can do it now so it doesn't need to be repeated. On Thursday, we indicated, or I indicated that -- sorry, Wednesday, indicated that so far as I was concerned, various things had to be resolved, and in relation to opening the case for Mr. Limaj, I was not in a position to give a definitive answer, possibly open but not very long. May I just indicate for your assistance that I would seek to open his case. I suspect it will take about one hour, and I'm having documents made available that you already have or should have, but I'm not sure whether they're still, as it were, within your purview. Secondly, Mr. Limaj himself would like to address the Tribunal, probably 20 to 30 minutes maximum. So I hope that's of some assistance. Otherwise, I don't have any other matter at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We have no matters at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the American in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There's no American in me. We should like if we may, please, after Mr. Mansfield, that is to say, therefore, in indictment order, to raise one or two matters on behalf of Mr. Musliu. He is extremely anxious and indeed specifically instructs that he would just like me to briefly revisit some matters that have been discussed in the past. They are, by way of headnote only, the circumstances of his initial arrest and detention, a word on the position regarding provisional release, incommunicado and touch upon blindfolds. May I also indicate, if it assists, that we propose to open the case. Our opening will take approximately 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it then only Mr. Mansfield is -- I take it that only Mr. Mansfield is minded to raise the matter of adjournment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, were you addressing me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was addressing Defence counsel generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry if I was not clear enough. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, no, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question is only Mr. Mansfield is to raise the question of adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There is an extant application before the Court in relation to -- Mr. Mansfield used the word postponement; I'll use Your Honour's word adjournment, which we put forward at the conference last week and which were treated for the purposes of the application as our application, and upon that the Chamber has yet to make a decision, or maybe it has made a decision but certainly none has been communicated. And consequently, as I understand it, Mr. Mansfield proposes to supplement those oral submissions this morning, and we would wish to hear what he has to say before, if at all, we add to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no decision has been made. We're aware of the issue and what we have seen in the written submissions so far, so I will turn to Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. I will -- I will endeavour not to reiterate the arguments and submissions put forward in the first place last week on behalf of Mr. Limaj, but inevitably there will be some echo of what was said then. Our concern is that the Prosecution, in their response, are attempting to minimise and marginalise the centrality of the allegation that has been made now for a very long time. And that is an important issue and an important factor. The allegation of witness intimidation put clearly at the door of these defendants, and in particular Mr. Limaj, surfaced in 2003, and we say that bears upon the obligation of the Prosecution to investigate it at that stage, and if there is evidence in particular linking any of these defendants in the sense of being responsible for any intimidation that may have occurred to be produced. The reason why it is now central is that the Prosecution indicated to Your Honour on the last conference before Your Honour the possibility, in fact it was put rather higher than that because the words used by the Prosecution were that they will introduce, subject to your ruling, material relating to this issue into the trial. Plainly if there were going to be no attempt to do so or no allegation, none of us would be concerned with this. One would be concerned but not from the point of view of preparation. And preparation, we say, is central to the case for this defendant, and all defendants plainly. It's, as you're aware, a right under -- under Article 6(3) that everyone should have time for proper preparation of their defence in relation to the issues in the case. And what the Prosecution have done is to raise this hare, as it were, and set it running and then say, well, whether it actually enters the main arena or the course of this trial just depends. It may, it may not, and we'll deal with it when it does, and we say this is entirely improper to do it in this way when it is central. Because -- and I think the one thing we did indicate last Wednesday is the allegation itself, especially against Mr. Limaj, mirrors the main allegations in the substantive case; namely that he is responsible for orchestrating threats and intimidation in the same way, no doubt, that the Prosecution will say in their opening he orchestrated and supervised the allegations of what went on at Lapusnik. So the two are running in parallel. And it's not just that mirror each other. Plainly, once that hare has been raised to Your Honour, it has a purpose. The purpose is in fact already predicated in the response, the latest response to these matters, because on page 6 of that latest response, the Prosecutor is already prophesying that if any evidence comes to light it would help explain deficiencies in the Prosecution case. In other words, it isn't just a question of going to the credibility of Mr. Limaj in the case, or even the culpability which they recognise might have a relevance to that in the case on the main issues, it will do that, say the Prosecution, but in addition, of course, they will want to say or at least even if they don't express it, they will leave it implicit in this exercise that any shortcomings in the evidence can be explained by the unspoken or sometimes spoken and sometimes attributed and sometimes unattributed allegations of intimidation. To put it specifically, if a witness does not attend, that's because there's been intimidation. If a witness doesn't come up to proof, that is because there has been intimidation. If a witness is inconsistent, that is because there's been intimidation. If a witness is diffident, it is because there has been intimidation. You can see it once exactly the role that this allegation is going to play in this case unless, we say, it is satisfactorily examined by which we mean at least the Defence given an opportunity to deal with this. The Prosecution on this topic say, oh, well, you can't prove a negative. Entirely missing the point. If in fact the allegation is, as it was originally, that there has been intimidation by Limaj directly or indirectly, and may I just quote the initial motion by the Prosecution this is a very important allegation put specifically in these terms. May I just read --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm terribly sorry to interrupt Mr. Mansfield, but might I point out that this is a confidential document. It may be the cat's out of the bag now, but confidential documents, my understanding, Mr. President, should be addressed in private session. It's not a public document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can rest relaxed that no cat has really emerged from any bag at the moment, Mr. Cayley. Thank you for your concern. Mr. Mansfield, are you going to the content of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I was going to indicate no names but just the terms in which it has been put against Limaj. In other words, directly and through others, and that the evidence specifically suggests, that kind of thing, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can manage that, Mr. Cayley, without any difficulty. Thank you for that, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: In fact, those are the words. In other words, essentially it was a clear, a concise, a suggestion that there was evidence at the availability and to the Prosecution that Limaj, either himself or through others, has used the communication facilities at the centre to do this. And in the motion to this hearing today and the document that we received last week, and may I say at once it's not that the Prosecution are only saying these matters in here. As you will have noticed, the Chief Prosecutor is making it very public, as she did in November. So this issue is being raised both publicly outside the Chamber and inside the Chamber. So the Defence begin a -- or are about to begin a trial in which there looms in the background not just a peripheral issue, because that's how the Prosecution are attempting to say, it is peripheral. We say that is a gross understatement. It's not peripheral. And they're trying to say on more than one occasion in their argument that this will have and does have no impact upon the Defence. They are entirely uninfected by it, and it's speculative. Well, given the terms in which the Prosecution were seeking disclosure, then we say it isn't speculative. It doesn't have a -- it doesn't lack impact. In fact, quite the reverse. Of course, interestingly the way that the Prosecution now put it is watered down. What they're now saying is that they believe that Limaj may have used the communications. That's not how they were putting it originally. In any event, we care not how they put it. Whether they're saying we have used or we may have used. It's very difficult to conceive of a way in which Limaj has orchestrated directly or indirectly without using the facilities, whether it be letter, whether it be telephone, whether it be direct contact with people from the Detention Unit. And the reason I raise it in forcible terms at this stage is that for two years the Prosecution have been in a position to deal with this matter so that we would know before we started, and certainly I say in Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond relation to Limaj, the material so far disclosed does not provide reasonable grounds for believing that Limaj has orchestrated anything. None of the material. Unless there's material that we haven't seen. But on the material that we have seen, there's nothing there to suggest that he has, and that is why we are anxious to dispel this so that both -- I appreciate your position; namely, you would be able to yourselves ignore material that you're not going to admit. However, we recognise and in the interests of justice being seen to be done that this cloud that has been raised is at least in part dispelled by giving us the opportunity to look at particular areas of time. Because, for example, in 2003, if it is suggested Limaj in some way or another was concerned with the incidents that had been set out at that time, and he was orchestrating it whilst in detention, then it shouldn't take too long to discover - and it should have been discovered before now - whether in fact he had had any part in that. Otherwise it forms no part of the allegation, and it forms no part of this case. And therefore, the facility -- and obviously we're not in a position to actually do it. The Prosecution are in a position to do it and we say should have done it before now in relation to that if that's going to be the suggestion. Either they have the evidence or it's just innuendo. And plainly the same matter arises again in the more recent past in relation to these allegations. And we say the reason why it is important not just to dispel in public as well as in the Tribunal so far as is possible this extraordinarily serious and invasive allegation, it will obviously be of considerable assistance to us when approaching witnesses because it is not clear so far which witnesses -- because we're only told of examples of interference, so is it to be said there are other ones which are not exemplified and which are known about but which will be introduced? It is important to know that before we start in order to, as it were, structure sensible investigation as well as cross-examination as well as submission. If it were a minor matter on the edge of this case, then plainly everyone is used to getting on with the business, as it were, and dealing with the matter. But this is a theme. It is underlying the case. This is the suggestion the Crown -- I'm so sorry, the Prosecution indicate what has infected this case. That is effectively where they haven't used that word what they say has happened. Well, they say, this can all be dealt with as we go along, and we say, once again, this is no way to, as it were, approach a responsible Prosecution, that we'll just deal with it when it turns up. And then there might be what, an adjournment during -- during the trial itself to deal with an allegation of this seriousness? Although there isn't a charge, it's very convenient, of course, that he hasn't been charged. We suggest if there is evidence against Limaj, then charge him. Let's face it. Let's deal with it. Join it with this case rather than leaving it there and say, well, we might join it later or, rather, we might have a separate charge later after this trial and so on. Again, if it was ancillary in the sense that it was allied but not important, one could understand that. If it was a minor allegation, one could understand it. It isn't. It doesn't be more serious. And no doubt the public will see it as a serious allegation as well. These are not, as it were, matters that can be remedied as we go along and as it's put a host of remedies which could be fashioned as appropriate such as recalling witnesses who have already been presumably cross-examined. That would be both inconvenient and upsetting and difficult for witnesses and also it means that questions would have to be re-tailored. This is all on the assumption, the Prosecution say, that of course they are going to find evidence or do they have it already against Limaj and it hasn't been disclosed. So the -- the suggestions of how to deal with this as we go along we say are totally unrealistic given the gravity of what is being suggested. So we do say that the response by the Prosecution in this case is entirely inadequate and misguided in the sense that it does not recognise the significance of what is being suggested here - repeatedly suggested - from 2003 right through to this moment. So we would ask, given the fundamental right to time to prepare, to deal with these allegations that we're not having to do it as we go along. As you know, it's difficult enough in a case of this kind with the amount of material, the difficulties of translation and so on, to really, as it were, pick it up and run with it as it appears, because we know not where the tentacles of this suggestion are going to end up. And we need to know now. Where are we going to end up with this suggestion, or is it all going to be left in the wings, dealt with in another trial, and you're left with an impression which will be very difficult to dispel, certainly in the public eye, that this has been put there for one reason only and that is, as it were, to poison the water. So we are very anxious that we're given at least an opportunity. Now, finally this: It is said by the Prosecution that we haven't put a time frame on it and that's -- it's difficult, because of course we don't know how much material is there. But we would ask for consideration of some time. Originally I was going to ask for at least 21 days to at least make a start on seeing what the categories of material are that to be disclosed and seeing whether amongst that material there is the slightest indication, because if there isn't, then we would want to -- I would want to put that in any opening that I make in relation to this. It's one of the most important prejudicial matters that has arisen that we would seek proper and fair, as it were, containment of this allegation. So certainly a time to give us an opportunity now that it is clear that it's a strong possibility that the Prosecution will want to introduce it. So that is how I put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mansfield. Mr. Guy-Smith, is there anything that you would wish to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We are somewhat differently situated than Mr. Limaj only in that no allegations whatsoever have been made against Mr. Bala in this regard. However, he has been tarred by the same brush repeatedly, and I fear that he, too, will suffer from the same forms of concerns that have been raised by Mr. Mansfield. I would join in his remarks and his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to that which has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Firstly, we would obviously repeat what we have already stated in our latest filing on this matter, but I will add a few remarks following on from what Mr. Mansfield has said. The three accused in this case have been in pre-trial custody for nearly two years. In February 2004, the Prosecutor stated that she was very keen indeed to get this matter to trial. That position still stands. We want to go to trial today. We want this trial to begin today. Witness intimidation in this case unfortunately is a fact. The motion of the 4th of November of 2004 sets out some of the facts concerning intimidation in this case. Prior to this time, and in fact Mr. Mansfield has used the same word today, Mr. Mansfield describes the allegations of witness intimidation as innuendo, malicious gossip on the part of the Prosecutor. Mr. Topolski described the allegations of witness intimidation as wild and baseless, and that was contained in his appeal to the President of this Tribunal in respect of the restriction on communications of the three accused. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I observe that on the material then available, as we have briefly seen it just recently, those observations might have been adequately and soundly founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On material that you've seen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That which was known to the Defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Judging on what we have been able to see, which is little of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm making the point that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- what is in your knowledge may be different from than which is in the knowledge of Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand the point. Subsequent to those particular comments, an indictment has been confirmed for contempt against another party, not a party in these proceedings, and indeed the President of the Tribunal upheld the decision of the Deputy Registrar to restrict communications. So in a sense an external audit of the evidence that the Prosecution has gathered on this particular issue has been, as it were, confirmed by, as I've stated, an external audit by two independent Judges. Now an application for adjournment is sought by the Defence on the eve of trial with the knowledge that these problems have gone back for the best part of a year, as Mr. Mansfield acknowledges. Oral submissions were is made on the 10th of November, as you know. The principal argument that the Defence are now running is that the issue of witness intimidation is central to the main case and so affects how the main case is run. Now, I am not going to enter into discussion about whether or not it is central to the main case or whether it is peripheral. What I would say strongly is that the main case here concerns an indictment alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity. That is the main case that we are dealing with here today. The issue of witness intimidation is important. I don't deny that. It is an important issue because it affects the administration of justice. And because within the Statute the protection of witnesses and their capacity to come forward before this court in a dignified and unburdened manner is a matter which is recognised by Article 20 of the Statute. Now, it's my view, Your Honours, that you must know what has taken place in respect of witness intimidation because the integrity of these proceedings depend upon it. But all of that does not warrant a delay in these proceedings. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just add a perspective that from the point of view of the Chamber, witness intimidation does not at all feature in the anticipated case. If it's in your mind, that may be a different thing. But at the moment, as far as the Chamber is aware, we are not dealing with evidence about witness intimidation. We are hearing a case about events that occurred a number of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I entirely agree with you that in that respect the evidence that you are going to hear is about war crimes and crimes against humanity, and upon that you will make your decision in this case. I agree with that. But it is my view, it is my submission that if witnesses are being interfered with, if that affects their ability to come before this Court in a dignified and unburdened fashion that is a matter you should know about at the proper time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you missed the point of my observation. At the moment, we know nothing of that in terms of the trial of these three accused on this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We of course are hearing submissions. Of course there have been related proceedings in the last short period, but they do not intrude into this trial and will only do so if you seek formally to have that occur whether there will be a question of whether it's in the interests of justice for that to be permitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And at that time, the Defence can make submissions before you that that evidence should not be admitted into the Chamber, if we were to decide to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your observations at the moment are suggesting that you have a clear thought that this will be an issue which will feature in your case. Now, if that's the position, it adds some significance to what Mr. Mansfield has been putting to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may become an issue. I cannot say that it will not. I cannot put the Prosecutor in that position with this issue. I cannot say it will not. It may become an issue in this case. The results of the telephone records, the release of the telephone records will, I think, go in one of two directions. They will either produce evidence that there has been interference with witnesses or they will produce nothing at all. Now, if they produce nothing at all, it doesn't affect the position of the Defence at all, because the allegation that was originally made about witness interference was not made prospectively by the Prosecutor in the hope that evidence might emerge from these telephone records. It was made upon the basis of evidence already in our possession. Now, if the telephone records do produce information or evidence that suggests that witnesses were interfered with, I wonder how that really helps the Defence. Is Mr. Mansfield going to put it to a witness who may have already given evidence in the case that because information is revealed by the telephone records that this particular witness was interfered with, is Mr. Mansfield going to put it to that witness? Is it right that you were interfered with and that somebody tried to prevent you giving evidence? I think that's a question that the Prosecution would put as opposed to the Defence. Now, as to the argument of the general environment, that there is a general environment of hostility and prejudice towards the two -- the three accused, I believe, Your Honours, that as professional Judges, you can divorce what you have heard or read about this issue from the main issues in this case, which is the evidence relating to war crimes and crimes against humanity, the matters addressed in the Second Amended Indictment. Now, the Defence have stated that if we sought to withdraw the motion of the 4th of November we should withdraw the allegation. Now, I want to make it perfectly clear we are not withdrawing the motion. The motion stands. And as I've already stated to you, the original allegation that was made was not based on an expectation that the telephone records might reveal information about witness intimidation. It was based on information already in our possession. The conduct of the Prosecution in this matter has been described by the Defence in their latest motion as cavalier. Now, I've always understood that word to mean arrogance or insolence. Perhaps it wasn't meant in that sense. Perhaps it was meant in the sense that we behaved irresponsibly. Whatever was meant, I would reassure this Court that we have conducted ourselves responsibly, cautiously, and for a purpose to ensure that this trial can actually take place. Your Honours, finally, delaying this case would actually assist the very purpose that the Prosecutor is seeking to avert. It would actually place witnesses at greater risk. It would exacerbate the position. The most effective way to deal with the issue of witness intimidation is for this trial to commence today and for the Prosecutor to complete her case in chief as soon as possible. Dealing with these telephone records is not going to take a day or a week or even two weeks. Mr. Mansfield has already stated 21 days. I suspect it will probably take months. Now, if that is the case, this case is going to be delayed for a very long time indeed. We do not want that. The Prosecutor wants to go to trial today. We do not intent on withdrawing our motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would like to hear you, Mr. Mansfield, on the other matters you planned to raise. We will, at a convenient time, then reflect upon what's been put to us on the question of an adjournment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. The -- thank you. I don't have a great deal to add on the other matters. I think I've already indicated the ambit of them, namely an opening of about an hour, and Mr. Limaj addressing you. I can't elaborate on either of those two, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can't. I'm sorry, I made a note and it may be my fault. I had a note you -- my note is of documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm so sorry. That was me indicating that in order to make it easier for you to follow what I'm saying there are a number of documents, and what we would like to do is assemble a file of the documents I intend to use so that you have them in front of each of you. They're documents that are before the Tribunal already but we just need time to assemble them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's for the purpose of the adjournment application.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, it isn't. It's for the purpose of the opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I have no other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith, you are not wishing to raise any matters. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I then deal I hope shortly with -- briefly, I mean, with the four matters I indicated before. May I preface them by saying this as I think I said to you on the last occasion that we met: My client came and sits there today with high regard for this Tribunal, or at least he came here with that high record. Four events over the last 20 months or so have for him undermined his confidence, and he wishes me here today, if you will, as I know you all will, hear me patiently just for a few moments to raise them again. He seeks this Tribunal's reassurance. They are these: He was arrested on the 11th of February, 2003, on a warrant issued by this Court on the 24th of January of that year, which required, as all warrants do, his timely transfer to this city, to this Tribunal. For six days of detention, the fact of that warrant was not disclosed to him. Thus he was held for six days ignorant of the reasons for or the justification of his detention. I do not take the Tribunal to an interview of him, but in the interview of him, indeed the first one with a representative of the investigator's office of this Tribunal, it is, in our submission, manifestly obvious that it is only then, that day, i.e., the 17th of February, that he is made aware of why he is held. What happened in these six days was that he was interrogated, interrogated unrepresented about matters not in this indictment nor, I add, in any other. The second point is this: Those events played a part, he believes - and may I underline the words he believes - in the refusal upon appeal of provisional release not being canvassed in open court and he not being given the opportunity as others have to voluntarily surrender to the jurisdiction of this court. The third matter is this: The material now disclosed that sought the incommunicado order places the allegations of orchestrating a campaign of witness interference very much at the door of Isak Musliu. I say now what I said before: Although they are not wild and baseless, because they have a base in evidence, they are vehemently denied from first to last. He regards one month before a trial notwithstanding the apparent force of that material that the decision to debar him from any contact with his family was Draconian and unnecessary and that the legitimate concern of the Prosecutor would have been, he says, and we submit, more appropriately met by something less Draconian than a complete communication ban. As I stand here today, that ban is now lifted. It's lifted because Mr. Cayley has not sought to reapply for it. It terminated over this past weekend. I only say this about blindfolds, the fourth and final matter, that when I saw him this morning in the cell, Isak Musliu was literally red-eyed and unable to speak to me without any degree of concentration about important matters I needed to talk to him about. The reason was yet again he had been blindfolded. I say no more than we await anxiously the final - and may I underline the word final - resolution of that. It's a comfort that this Tribunal had understood the position this morning, a particular comfort because we have not even had the courtesy of a reply from the Registrar as to the letter you, Your Honour, invited us to make -- write on the last occasion we were before you seeking their assistance. They are the four matters I wish to raise. We're grateful for the patience with which the Court has sat and listened to them. They are an attempt to clear the air. He still, as I said, holds this Tribunal in high regard. As to where we go from here this morning, we shall see, but they are the matters I wish to raise on his behalf at the moment. With just one addition, if I may, to flag up a very considerable difficulty we are having with interpreters. May I tell the Court that I could not see Isak Musliu for the entirety of last week in the Detention Unit, having come to move to The Hague last week for the purpose of seeing him upon a regular basis. Why not? Because I was only offered the services of interpreter but for a very limited period of time during the course of -- sorry, the week before last. I beg your pardon. I saw him last week. The week before last. There was a complete de facto inability of us to see our client two weeks before this trial was to start because there were not enough Albanian-speaking interpreters. I don't think this is going to be the last time this is going to be raised but I flag it up as a potential serious and ongoing difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are these interpreters ones that you are providing for the purposes of Defence preparation or are you speaking of Tribunal interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith is the resident expert on interpreters at counsel's bench. So I wonder if I may invite him to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The interpreters that we have are for the sole purpose of Defence preparation. The gentleman who sits beside me today I was fortunate enough to have come for the first time to these proceedings for today. He will be with us today and half of tomorrow. After that, depending on what further success we have, we may or may not have an interpreter in this courtroom for the balance of the week. This has been a continued problem. It has been an a severe problem. It is a problem that I know Mr. Topolski suffered, I believe Mr. Mansfield and Mr. Khan suffered, and I, too, have suffered. I was incapable of seeing my client last week while at the detention centre, and I had, I believe, it was two of my visits terminated because there was not an individual for me to use for purposes of interpretation and translation. At one point in time, I was fortunate enough to be able to use the services of a gentleman who works inside the Detention Unit, which was hardly satisfactory, but at least it got us through a bit of a conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's still obscure to me at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't mean to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- is whether you are speaking of an expectation there be provided to you Tribunal interpreters, or is it that you are saying the Defence is having difficulty finding interpreters for its own purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We had been led to believe in - and perhaps mistakenly so - that the Tribunal would be in a position to provide interpreters for us. However, I have been informed as a result of a training session I was in that the Tribunal itself is having difficulty in regard to the language of Albanian. It is apparently quite a unique language and, as I was informed as were others in the same meeting, the market is small. Therefore, in direct response to your question, Your Honour, we the Defence are having a phenomenally difficult time finding individuals who are either, one, willing, or two, qualified. And the willingness has to do with economic considerations because of the payment structure that exists for those people which they find to be well below what they should expect and well below what the going rate is. However, I don't know how far you wish for me to continue in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've now answered clearly, thank you. As I understand the position, funds have been allocated as part of what I might call the legal aid programme for the purposes of the Defence arranging interpretation for its own confidential purposes. And from what I understand, your difficulty is that you cannot find people who are able to undertake that work at the sort of remuneration level that you have readily available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is one of the concerns. The second concern is, as I indicated previously, the market is small. There are not that many people who actually speak the Albanian language and English sufficiently in this particular area to be able to be utilised for purposes of Defence preparation. I personally have gone far and wide in an attempt to find people who could fulfil this function, including interviews in London as well as interviews in Kosovo. However, the amount that it would cost to have those people come here, live here for the sole purpose of translation is prohibitive and well outside of those funds that have been allocated for purposes of interpretation. I believe there is an expectation that there is a -- there are people here who are in a position to fulfil this function, and unfortunately I'm not finding that to be the case, but I continue to endeavour in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We wish you well in those endeavours, Mr. Guy-Smith, and Mr. Topolski as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber proposes to have a short adjournment now for the purpose of giving consideration to the substantial matter that has been raised with us of the question of adjournment. I'd expect we will be in a position to return and advise all concerned of our decision in about a quarter of an hour from now. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that there is not sufficient justification for a delay to the start of the trial. The witness -- the issue of witness intimidation is not a fresh development, although for the first time there are formal proceedings. An indictment has issued, but it is not against any one of the present accused, and it is not presently the position of the Prosecution that any one of the accused or more are involved in that other case. There is no proposal presently before the Chamber to introduce into this trial evidence of witness intimidation involving any one of the accused. The position really is that there is conjecture. There is the possibility, should yet unknown evidence materialise, that the Prosecution might seek to introduce into this trial evidence of witness intimidation. Just what that evidence might be is presently unknown and unpredictable. If that should occur, the time will then arise, in the Chamber's view, for a consideration of whether that should be allowed and, if so, what the interests of justice may require. At this point it is simply conjectural. As far as the Chamber can presently foresee, should that arise and should there be justification for the evidence to be introduced into this trial, the range of measures that are available to the Chamber should be adequate to ensure that the interests of justice in this trial are adequately protected. We recognise, as has been put to us by Mr. Mansfield, that the position to be taken by those representing the accused in their defence might be more certainly and better shaped were it known exactly at this point what, if any, evidence were to be introduced in this trial. That, though, in the circumstances, is not a realistic expectation, because the nature of recent events suggest that if there is any development, and that's merely conjectural, it is something that will not occur in the very near future, and there can be little or no present prospect that merely by an adjournment of one or two or even three weeks, as suggested, that those representing the accused could be assured that they were in a position of knowing all that might possibly arise in this regard in the conduct of this trial. Clearly the longer the time passes, as we move into the trial, the more significant would be any proposal to introduce this evidence and the more difficult would be the prospect of such a proposal succeeding. For these brief reasons, we will commence the trial this afternoon as planned. Mr. Mansfield sought some indulgence in respect of documentation. We would indicate that we would not expect to hear you until tomorrow. That may, I hope, be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seem to be no further issues that require attention at this point. The Prosecution witness list is presently complete. It is not the present intention of this Chamber, as sometimes occurs in this jurisdiction, to indicate precise time constraints on the presentation of the Prosecution case, just as it will not be our present intention to do that for the Defence. We will, however, be mindful of the rate of progress, and if serious concern arises, we may then feel the need to take measures. We will adjourn now until 2.15.
